newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's BHP reads Riot Act on poor assets.
newsitem.headline: Australia's BHP reads Riot Act on poor assets.

text.p: Australia's largest listed company, The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd (BHP), on Monday said it could no longer tolerate poorly performing assets and would get rid of them out if they did not shape up.
The steel, mining and petroleum group's senior executives told a briefing seminar that about 10 percent of the company's US$29 billion worth of assets were not pulling their weight.
"They've got to improve or they've got to go," managing director John Prescott told reporters covering the seminar.
In a frank assessment of its own performance, the executives told share analysts and fund managers that returns on capital and equity for the group were inadequate.
"Returns being achieved currently are not acceptable," BHP's executive general manager for finance, Graeme McGregor, said.

Last Friday, BHP reported a 61 percent dive in net profit to A$410 million (US$307 million) for the year ended May 31, its worst bottom-line result in a decade, after almost A$1 billion in one-off losses.
The losses stemmed mainly from BHP's decision to slice the value of underperforming assets, including a A$550 million write-down of its recently acquired U.S. copper operations.
In 12 months, the group's five divisions of steel, minerals, copper, petroleum and services have been told their assets need to return at least 10 percent return on capital.
Otherwise, McGregor told the seminar, "action will be taken to lift returns or the asset will be sold".
One share analyst has predicted BHP would sell assets of around A$1.5 billion in the current 1997/98 year.
BHP has said it expects no more abnormal write-downs in 1997/98 and that it is confident the group will lift its financial performance substantially over the next three years.
But in part recognition of BHP's increased exposure to the world copper price, the world's second biggest copper producer has adopted a new set of performance benchmarks for the group.
BHP confirmed on Monday it no longer aimed for a 15 percent return on equity and instead strived to be among the world's best 20 percent of companies in terms of shareholder returns.
BHP takes into account both dividends and growth in its share price to measure returns to shareholders.

"The objective is to achieve a result that's comparable with what the best companies achieve, and the best companies are taken from all companies, not just companies in our sector," managing director Prescott told the seminar.
"The purpose of abandoning the percentages (targets) is to recognise that there is volatility in our markets."
BHP is bullish on the near-term outlook for copper despite a recent dip in the spot price and, for the first time in months, took the offensive regarding its embattled copper division.

It said cash costs at its majority-owned Escondida mine in Chile -- one of its top assets -- were competitive at an average 47 U.S. cents per pound and, at a more refined stage, it was producing copper for about 57 cents a pound.
The current world refined price is around US$1.11 a pound.
BHP also outlined plans to spend US$40 million to rework its San Manuel copper smelter in Arizona, which accounts for about 25 percent of total copper output in the United States.

Even the weather is at last smiling on BHP Copper. Reuters reported on Monday that rain had finally brought its Ok Tedi mine in Papua New Guinea back to life after a drought dried up its lifeline, the Fly River, which is used to ferry supplies.
BHP said on Monday it planned to lower its debt-to-equity ratio, but it would keep investing in its future with A$4.5 billion in capital expenditure budgeted for 1997/98 alone.
BHP's Prescott wrapped up the seminar by saying major change was needed across the group, to lift its performance.
"It's not business as usual at BHP," he said. "We are a company in transition."
But one analyst, who sought anonymity, on Monday said BHP still had to match all of its words with deeds.
"It's a big step from saying you are going to do something to actually doing it," he told Reuters.
